cia-0000119713: A May 1953 CIA paper forecasts probable developments in Indonesia. The young republic faced revolts in its regions and disorder in its parliament. Washington counted the islands a Cold War prize, and the paper weighs where the country might turn. The republic was only a few years old, and its hold on the outer islands was still being tested when the forecast was written.
cia-0000124313: Dated July 1951, this CIA document addresses Communist treatment of United Nations prisoners, with the word treatment misspelled in the original heading. The error survived into the released file along with the substance. The paper records that treatment as the agency understood it then. Treatment reports fed the public argument over the war at home, where stories from the camps shaped how Americans judged both the enemy and the armistice talks.
cia-0000132213: From January 1991, situation report 530 covers political developments including a Baghdad radio call, the heading breaking off. Iraqi state radio served as Saddam's mouthpiece to the world during the crisis. The report notes what the broadcast said that day. Baghdad radio was heard worldwide through monitoring services, and a call noted in a sitrep usually meant a message aimed at Iraqis and enemies at once.
cia-0000132413:
A break in relations between the Castro government and the United States is weighed in a CIA report dated October 3, 1959. The report treats the rupture as a real possibility. The open question was when it might come, not whether feelings were souring.

Inside, analysts weigh the signs pointing toward a formal break. Relations did in fact end in January 1961, little more than a year later. For readers, the report is an early marker of how soon the agency saw the end coming. It shows the split being forecast while public ties between the two countries still held.
cia-0000132513:
Fallout for the United States from a failed attack on the Castro regime fills a CIA document dated April 5, 1961. Its headline calls the findings preliminary, and the title breaks off before finishing that word. The failed attack it names already lay in the past when analysts wrote.

The document assesses what the attempt cost and what it changed. Coming twelve days before the Bay of Pigs landing, it reads as a warning from a smaller failure. For readers, it shows the agency studying defeat in Cuba once already. The larger defeat that followed that month would echo many of the same lessons.
cia-0000132613: Haiti seeking closer ties with Cuba fills item 4 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated July 5, 1960. The pairing was an odd one: a harsh dictatorship courting a young revolution. Duvalier's Haiti was hunting for friends wherever they could be found that year. The short item reports the outreach and what Haiti hoped it might bring.
cia-0000135813: The declassified CIA document dated 1 February 1954 takes up political action talks and debriefings, with the names in the heading deleted by the censors. Behind the paper stands PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA campaign against President Arbenz that closed with the 1954 coup in Guatemala. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000135913: Filed on 4 May 1954, this CIA meeting record concerns a report of meetings with undisclosed persons, written as the situation began to change. All of it feeds into PBSUCCESS, the agency operation against the Arbenz government in the months before the June 1954 coup. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000136113: One declassified cable from the CIA files, dated 4 April 1954, covers a review of a report that urged playing the waiting game, patience weighed against speed. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136313: Radio material from 1400 to 2300 hours is summarized in this 26 June 1954 LINCOLN cable. Castillo asked that Chajon attack Zacapa at 0800 the next day in a synchronized action, and that planes find and bomb enemy artillery near Cumbre Ingeniero. A delayed message from another operator called the situation very bad, with enemy units reported at Entre Rios, Morales, and Champona. The summary captures the confused final days of the Arbenz government.
un-ga-res-a-69-13: Joint work with a Black Sea trade bloc fills Resolution A/69/13, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Black Sea Economic Cooperation Organization has held observer status at the Assembly since 1999. The text recalls past votes on the tie, the last in 2012, and the Assembly's 1994 call for stronger UN work with regional groups. Any strife in the region, it warns, holds back joint work of this kind.
un-ga-res-13:
Eight great offices formed the spine of the first UN Secretariat, under Resolution 13 of the General Assembly, from February 1946. The office setup, the text holds, must let the work run with the greatest speed and thrift. The Secretary-General must build that setup at once. It must let him meet his duties under the Charter and serve the needs of all the UN's arms.

The chief units are named: arms for Security Council affairs, trade and wealth, social work, and lands not yet free. Public facts, law, meetings and services, and the money office round out the list. Assistant chiefs may be named to run them. The chart drawn here still shapes the UN's vast staff today.
un-sc-res-113:
By April 1956, the steps the Security Council had ordered to ease tension along the armistice lines in Palestine had still not been carried out. Resolution 113, adopted without dissent on 4 April 1956, says the situation between the parties is now likely to endanger peace and security.

Instead of issuing new orders, the Council turns to fact-finding. It asks the Secretary-General, as a matter of urgent concern, to survey how the four General Armistice Agreements are being enforced and how its own past resolutions are being obeyed. He is also to arrange with the parties, after talks with them and with the Chief of Staff, any measures that could cut the tension.
un-sc-res-713: The record catalogued as Resolution 713, dated 1991, preserves one formal decision of the United Nations Security Council. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1913: Resolution 1913 is a formal Security Council decision held in this collection through a transcription of the UN's official record. Its opening clauses establish the members' shared view of the matter; its numbered clauses establish their shared command. The entry preserves both establishments whole, which is what makes it a primary source rather than a reference note.
cia-0000135613: Brigade 2506's declassified Spanish files hold this document, dated 5 March 1961. The exile brigade was then in its last weeks of preparation for the April landing in Cuba. Nothing in the catalog record states what this document covers, who wrote it, or which unit it came from. It stands as a dated primary source in the original Spanish, released by the CIA, and any account of its contents must come from reading it rather than from its file title.
cia-0000135713: This Spanish text, dated 2 February 1961, belongs to the 2506 Brigade document set released by the CIA. The brigade was then in final training for the invasion of Cuba. The catalog title is generic, offering no subject, author, or unit. The document is kept in Spanish as a primary source. Its date places it among the last records of the training period, weeks before the brigade sailed.
cia-0000136613: A Spanish-language paper dated 4 January 1961, filed with the 2506 Brigade documents released by the CIA. It shares its date with companion items in the same stretch of the file. The exile brigade was in winter training for the April landing. The catalog names no subject for this document. Preserved in Spanish, it is part of the dense early-January layer of the brigade's surviving paperwork.
cia-0000136713: A Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers, cataloged under an estimated date of 5 January 1960. That is strikingly early for this file, since the brigade was formed during 1960; the estimated flag in the title is part of the record and worth noting. No subject is named for the document. It survives in Spanish in the CIA's declassified release, dated by estimate to the brigade's first days or before them.
plos-pone-0000013:
Pia Leppänen, Ivana Kholová, Anssi Mähönen, and co-authors switched on a growth gene in mice and watched what happened over time. The gene makes hVEGF-A165, a signal that tells the body to grow new blood vessels. In their transgenic mice, a Cre switch let them activate the gene in chosen tissue, then track short and long-term effects.

Vessel growth is a double-edged tool: it can heal starved tissue, but it can also feed tumors or leak and swell. Seeing both the early response and the lasting state of the tissue shows where the risks settle. The study informs gene therapy plans that hope to use this same signal in patients.
cia-0000137313: NSC Briefing — Cuba, dated 1960, is a declassified CIA briefing for the National Security Council, the body that advises the president on security policy. Cuba dominated that council's agenda in 1960 as Castro's government turned toward Moscow and against Washington. A group of near-identical Cuba briefings from 1960 survives in these files, and the catalog does not set this one's contents apart from theirs. It is best read as part of that run: the steady flow of Cuba papers reaching the top of the U.S. government that year.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d13: Roosevelt replied to Churchill on June 28, 1943, and the message stands as Document 13 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The same day produced a Churchill note in return, a sign of how fast the exchange moved that week. The record lists the parties and the date only. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d113: On November 10, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, and his message is Document 113 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The two leaders wrote almost daily that week, even with a meeting a fortnight ahead, because the plans for two conferences still had loose ends. The record gives the date and the names and no subject. The message survives in the Foreign Relations series' pre-departure papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d213:
The Joint Staff Planners sent report J.C.S. 600 to the Joint Chiefs of Staff on 11 November 1943. Its subject is airfields for very-long-range B-29 bombers in the China-Burma-India area, tying the question to the decisions taken at the Quebec conference that August.

The planners say B-29s could be ready early in 1944, and that attacks on Japan could start sooner if fields were built in time. They call for at least four fields near Calcutta and five near Chengtu in China, built with British and Chinese help. Their recommendation is that all nine be authorized and finished, as far as possible, by May 1944.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d313:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 410 at Cairo on 25 November 1943, an examination of how weather limits any postponement of Operation Overlord, the cross-Channel invasion of France. It was ammunition in the Anglo-American argument over the invasion's date.

The assault needs a quiet spell of four days with winds of force three or less. Counting ten years of weather, such spells came eighteen times in April and twenty-one in May. They came nineteen times in June, and still seventeen in September. On the assault alone, the operation could slip to September. The build-up after landing needs about three months of workable weather. Tides confine each attempt to two short windows a month, and missing the full-moon window, needed for the air lift, costs twenty-four days.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d413:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent Ambassador Harriman a confidential telegram, numbers 1342 to 1344, from Washington at midnight on 4 December 1943. It reports the uproar in the American press over Moscow's early announcement of the Tehran Conference.

Morning papers in the United States headlined London stories about a Moscow radio broadcast. The broadcast, an official Soviet news agency one for provincial papers, had announced the Tehran meeting. It spoke of talks on the war against Germany and on political questions. Decisions, it said, would be made public later. No word of the conference's end had reached America, and Washington had nothing to announce. Hull says the publication has created a furor. Elmer Davis of the Office of War Information asks the department to learn one thing: whether the broadcast broke any release date the conferees had agreed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d513:
Laurence Steinhardt, the American ambassador in Ankara, reported to Secretary of State Hull on December 9, 1943. Days earlier, Roosevelt and Churchill had met Turkey's President İnönü at Cairo and failed to bring Turkey straight into the war. The State Department printed Steinhardt's message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Steinhardt's post gave him the Turkish view of that refusal: what Ankara feared, what it wanted, and what it might still do. Reports from the man on the spot guided Washington's next steps with a neutral country the Allies badly wanted. For readers, the message continues the Turkish story beyond the conference room doors.
frus-1944-quebec-d13:
Representatives of the British Chiefs of Staff in Washington prepared this memorandum on July 14, 1944. The British Joint Staff Mission in Washington kept London's military views in front of the American chiefs between conferences. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Staff missions did the alliance's daily military diplomacy: papers exchanged, positions tested, and disputes cooled before they reached the leaders. A July memorandum from the British mission belongs to the preparation of the autumn's great questions, which the Quebec Conference would settle in September. For readers, it shows the professional layer where allied strategy was drafted before it was decided.
frus-1944-quebec-d113:
An editors' note in the Quebec Conference volume points readers to records from August 1944 about aid to the Polish underground army. That force had risen against the Germans in Warsaw as the Soviet army neared the city. The note lists the published sources where the full documentation on the episode can be found.

The note also records an unresolved detail. President Raczkiewicz of Poland had written to Roosevelt on August 12, and a reply was drafted on August 31. No copy of that reply was ever found in American files. It was sent by pouch to London on September 8. The note shows the volume's editors flagging a gap in the record rather than hiding it.
frus-1944-quebec-d213:
Hull forwarded two enclosures to Roosevelt on September 11, 1944. One was Ambassador Winant's telegram on the European Advisory Commission. The other was the draft protocol on occupation zones in Germany and the administration of Greater Berlin. Gousev was ready to recommend acceptance of the zones protocol with one gap: the American and British zones left blank, for the two governments to decide themselves. frus-1945-malta-yalta-d113:

Maisky, the Soviet ambassador, had set out two roads. One divided Europe into eastern and western fields of chief concern. The other had the three nations work as one to destroy fascist rule and rebuild a Europe at peace. His government, he said, chose the second road. frus-1945-malta-yalta-d213:

A world body should govern the Rhine region, its south held by France alone and its north under mixed control. Germany must be cut down so she can never wage war again. But, Bidault added, he would not like a red flag over Germany to be followed by a black one, the pirate's flag. He also spoke with sympathy of the Security Council voting plan.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d313:

frus-1945-malta-yalta-d413:

frus-1945-potsdam-1-d13:

frus-1945-potsdam-1-d113:

frus-1945-potsdam-1-d213:

frus-1945-potsdam-1-d313:

frus-1945-potsdam-1-d413:

frus-1945-potsdam-1-d513:

frus-1945-potsdam-1-d613:

frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-13:

John Henry Newman wrote An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine in 1845 while leaving Anglicanism for Rome. Development, he argues, is not corruption but life: a living idea grows, and tests can distinguish healthy growth from decay. He applies those tests to Roman Catholic claims against his former church. Dense and brilliant, the essay is among the most consequential religious books of the nineteenth century, and Newman converted as he finished it.

babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-13:

nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-13:
Volume thirteen of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, gathers Chrysostom's homilies on eight of Paul's letters: Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, Thessalonians, Timothy, Titus, and Philemon. It also shows how the early church read nearly the whole of Paul in public worship.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-13:
Volume thirteen of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890, holds more of Gregory the Great, then turns east: Ephraim Syrus and Aphrahat, the Persian sage. Schaff and Wace edited the series. The Syriac fathers here wrote in the language of Jesus's own country.

Gregory's later letters and his book of dialogues, full of Italian saints and wonders, open the volume. Ephraim, the fourth-century deacon of Edessa, then sings the faith in hymns of unmatched imagery; the English here is prose, but the music shows through. Aphrahat's demonstrations, written under Persian rule, are the earliest Syriac theology we have. The volume is the series' window on the eastern church.
dawson-woodward-piltdown-1913:
Charles Dawson and Arthur Smith Woodward presented the Piltdown finds to the Geological Society in 1913. Gravel pits at Piltdown in Sussex had produced skull pieces and a jaw. They named the supposed creature Eoanthropus dawsoni, Dawson's dawn man.

The authors describe a big-brained skull paired with an ape-like jaw. Britain celebrated a first Englishman of great antiquity. Forty years later, tests exposed the bones as a planted forgery. The paper remains history's most famous scientific fraud, read now as a warning about wishful thinking. Schoolbooks repeated the dawn-man story for the next forty years.
potts-wonderfull-discoverie-lancaster-16:
Thomas Potts served as clerk of the court when twelve people faced witchcraft charges at Lancaster in 1612. His Wonderfull Discoverie of Witches in the Countie of Lancaster came out in 1613. It is the court's own account of the Pendle trials, England's best-known witch case.

Potts records the charges, the proof, and the words of the accused as the assizes heard them. Ten of the twelve were hanged, among them women from the Pendle Hill country. A child witness helped doom her own kin. The book still gives the fullest sense of how such a trial ran, step by step.
witches-apprehended-examined-executed-16:

The guide tells readers what marks, acts, and signs should raise alarm in their own towns. That pairing is the point of the print, and it was a shrewd one. Trial news taught fear, and the guide taught readers how to act on it. The pamphlet shows charge and belief feeding each other in Jacobean England.
cato-de-agri-cultura-harrison-1913:
Cato the Elder set down the oldest Latin prose that survives in his farm book, De Agri Cultura. Cato on Farming, in Fairfax Harrison's 1913 English rendering, gives the stern Roman's manual whole. Cato wrote in the second century before Christ, as Rome grew rich and hard.

The book mixes plain farm rules with praise of the farming life and scorn for soft city ways. Cato tells how to buy land, plant vines, feed slaves, and time the year's work. His short, blunt sentences set the tone of Latin prose at its birth. The manual opens the whole Latin literary tradition.
charles-apocrypha-pseudepigrapha-ot-vol2:
Robert Charles gathered the great Jewish writings left out of the Bible in his landmark edition of 1913. The Apocrypha and Pseudepigrapha of the Old Testament, volume two, holds the Pseudepigrapha in English. These are works written in the names of old heroes like Enoch and Ezra.

Jubilees, the books of Enoch, the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, Baruch, Fourth Ezra, and the Psalms of Solomon all stand here. They tell of angels, last days, and the hopes of Jews under foreign rule. Charles's notes made the hard texts plain to English readers. The volume stayed the scholar's standard for most of a century.
nukariya-religion-of-the-samurai-1913:
Kaiten Nukariya, a Japanese Zen scholar of the Soto school, wrote for Western readers in 1913. The Religion of the Samurai sets out Zen thought and training as it grew in China and Japan. No earlier English book by a Japanese Zen teacher had reached so far.

Nukariya tells the rise of Zen, its view of mind and world, and the hard drill of sitting and koan work. He shows how the warrior class of Japan took Zen as its inner rule of life. His tone is calm, clear, and free of mystic fog. The book first opened Zen to the English-speaking world.
crowley-book-of-lies-1913:
Ninety-three short chapters make up Crowley's Book of Lies, printed in 1913. Each chapter is a paradox, a jest, a riddle, or a brief shock of prose or verse. The book is also called, in jest, Breaks, and its full title warns the reader not to trust it.

Crowley said each chapter held a truth that flat statement would spoil. Thelemites have read the squibs as doctrine, as humor, and as traps for the too-literal mind. Few of his books have drawn so much commentary line by line. It remains the central Thelemic book of wit and contradiction.
crowley-book-4-part-2-1913:

The temple, the circle, the triangle, and the wand, cup, sword, and pantacle are each defined and placed. Crowley tells what each tool means and why the plan of the rite takes its shape. The book made his magic a teachable craft with clear rules and reasons. It is the working mate to part one's mystic training.
poincare-foundations-of-science-1913:
Henri Poincare, a French sage of maths and deep thought, wrote three books on the nature of science. George Halsted turned all three into English, and this set came out in 1913. The parts are Science and Hypothesis, The Value of Science, and Science and Method.

Poincare asks what a law of nature is, and how much of it men make by choice. He states a rule of relativity much like the one Einstein would make famed soon after. The set is science at thought on its own base, by one of its great minds.
munro-prehistoric-britain-1913: Robert Munro wrote this short survey of the deep past of Britain for the Home University Library in 1913. The set was made to put sound learning in the hands of plain readers. Munro was a Scots doctor who had dug much of his own proof in the field. In a small compass he sets out the stone age case for the isles, from flint tools to cave finds. It is the clear word on the deep past as its age knew it.
maunder-planets-inhabited-1913:
E. Walter Maunder was a star man at Greenwich who knew Mars well. His book Are the Planets Inhabited? came out in 1913. He wrote it to test the claims of Percival Lowell. Lowell held that wise beings built canals on Mars.

Maunder shows how the eye can join dots and blobs into false straight lines. He weighs heat, air, and water on Mars and finds them thin and harsh. His calm case broke the back of the canal tale. The book marks the turn when most star men gave up a peopled Mars.
bragdon-primer-higher-space-1913:
Claude Bragdon was an architect with a deep love of theosophy and form. His Primer of Higher Space came out in 1913. Cuts and clear plates show the fourth dimension in a way the eye can grasp. Bragdon hoped to lift the mind past flat, dull views of space.

He starts with points, lines, and planes, then steps up to the tesseract. Art, faith, and the soul all take on new shape in his scheme. The book took talk of higher space to artists and occult readers. Its fine plates still catch the eye of new fans today.
levi-history-of-magic-waite-1913:
Eliphas Levi was the pen name of a French occult scribe of the 1800s. A. E. Waite gave his History of Magic English dress in 1913. The book sweeps the whole tale of magic from old times to Levi's day. It is the tale that framed the new occult age.

Mystery cults of Greece and Egypt open the long march. Templars, alchemists, and Rosicrucians take their turns in the line. Levi holds that one hid lore runs through all the ages. His grand sweep gave the occult world a past it could claim as its own.
ouspensky-symbolism-of-the-tarot-1913:
P. D. Ouspensky wrote The Symbolism of the Tarot in 1913. Ouspensky was a Russian thinker drawn to hid lore and higher space. The book reads the tarot pack as a scheme of signs. Its heart is the set of two and twenty great cards, the Major Arcana.

Card by card, he draws out the sense of the Fool, the Magus, and the World. Each card, he holds, holds a key truth on man and the cosmos. The tone is that of thought, not of fate tells for pay. The book is a chief text of the tarot as a path of the mind.
avalon-tantra-great-liberation-1913:

Rites, hymns, and rules for the life of the faith fill the text. The work dates from a late age of the Tantra line. Woodroffe adds long notes to clear hard points for new readers. The book is the root work of all Tantra study in the West since.
charles-apocrypha-pseudepigrapha-1913:

doyle-poison-belt-1913:

devisser-dragon-in-china-and-japan-1913:

langhorne-plutarch-lives-vol-2-1813:

langhorne-plutarch-lives-vol-3-1813:

langhorne-plutarch-lives-vol-4-1813:

War and state craft form the meat of most lives in the book. Plutarch sets the two men of each pair side by side at the close. His aim is to teach by lives, not to write a dry roll of the past. The dress reads smooth and grave, fit for the theme.
langhorne-plutarch-lives-vol-5-1813:

Kings, orators, and men of war fill the pairs of this book. Each life ends with a weigh up of the two men in one view. Plutarch's love of small tales that bare the soul marks each life. The set held its place in homes and schools for a long span.
langhorne-plutarch-lives-vol-6-1813:

austen-pride-and-prejudice-1813:
Jane Austen published Pride and Prejudice in 1813, in the first edition text used here. The novel of Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy became her most beloved work. Austen wrote it in her twenties and reworked it before it reached print at last.

Elizabeth, sharp and poor, must find a husband or face a bleak future. Darcy seems proud and cold, and first talks between them spark and clash. Letters, visits, and a scandal with Wickham slowly show both their true worth. Pride falls on one side and prejudice on the other, in fine balance. lawrence-sons-and-lovers-1913:
