plos-pone-0004813: Anthrax in North America was assumed to be a colonial import. Kenefic and colleagues present genetic evidence for pre-Columbian origins, tied to ancient human migrations. The findings rewrite the pathogen's American history. Disease ecology with deep time depth, spanning millennia.
plos-pone-0005413: A Bornean frog sings fully in echo scans, a first for frogs. Arch and team showed Huia cavitympanum uses purely super-high calls for communication, proven by playback experiments. The frogs hear what we cannot. Super-high love songs in the jungle canopy.
plos-pone-0005513: Pseudomonas forms floating aggregates resembling suspended biofilms. Schleheck and team showed PAO1 grows as aggregates in liquid culture and disperses when starved. The conduct shows biofilm-like life without surfaces. Germs clumping for staying alive, then scattering, a new model for studying biofilm dispersal.
plos-pone-0005613: Kaposi sarcoma virus spreads fast among newly HIV-infected people. Batista and colleagues documented high HHV-8 prevalence and incidence in Sao Paulo. The epidemiology guides prevention. Tracking a cancer virus in Brazil's largest city, public health for a neglected co-infection.
plos-pone-0005713: Cells without mitochondrial DNA face an energy crisis. Mineri and colleagues studied how human cells react to mtDNA loss. The response reveals nuclear-mitochondrial crosstalk. Life without the mitochondrial genome, experimentally, cell biology of energy failure, two genomes in one cell, with rho-zero cells telling their story.
plos-pone-0005813: Mammary glands need Wnt signal to develop. Lindvall and team showed Lrp6 is required for normal mouse mammary growth. The co-sensor's role complements Lrp5. Building breasts' blueprint, sensor by sensor, ductal stem cells' signal needs, biology of the mammary gland.
plos-pone-0006413: Cell nuclei need their shield. Markovic and team drained nuclear glutathione in 3t3 skin cells and growth stalled. The nucleus pool guards splitting — growth's hidden fuel, found, in mouse cells studied. Debate settled in part: life's must-have, and splitting needs the pool.
plos-pone-0006513: Notes on paper boost memory. Zhang and Wang found outside records stretch working memory's limits. The page extends the mind — thinking with props, tested, where memory aids are probed. Task scores weighed, room expanded: few direct tests, in a tweaking study, where aids help.
plos-pone-0006613: Notch receptors need one clean cut. Gordon and team found S1 cleavage shapes Notch1 and Notch2 build, export, and signals. The cut's triple role — signals' growing up snip, mapped, via a furin-like cutter. Twin formed, NRR region: negative control, surface delivery.
plos-pone-0009413: A jumping gene called IS1301 lands inside the capsule-making machinery of meningitis-causing bacteria, and earlier work showed it helps Spanish strains survive immune attack. This study widens the picture, testing how the insertion affects both harmless carriage in the throat and full-blown disease. The findings connect a single genetic hop to the difference between a quiet resident and a killer.
plos-pone-0009513: Bacteria coordinate their genes through regulatory networks we have only partly mapped. This paper uses Bayesian network expansion on gene-activity data to predict missing links, uncovering new regulators of oxidative stress responses and biofilms. The method turns piles of microarray data into testable wiring diagrams of the cell.
plos-pone-0009613: HIV smuggles its genetic material out of the nucleus using a viral protein called Rev — but a human protein, DDX3X, gets in the way. This study examines how evolutionary constraints on DDX3X interfere with that escape route. The paper exposes a human roadblock in the virus's supply chain.
plos-pone-0010413: Cerebral malaria kills children, and platelets make it worse. This study shows a platelet protein, PF4, controls the KLF4 switch in monocytes during experimental brain malaria. The paper maps a platelet-immune crosstalk that could be interrupted to save young lives.
plos-pone-0010513: T cells grip their targets through the integrin LFA-1, supposedly regulated by calpain proteases. This study finds calpain 4 isn't needed after all. The paper corrects the record on immune cell adhesion, simplifying the textbook picture. The correction trims an unnecessary player from the adhesion story.
plos-pone-0010613: We work to prolong pleasant experiences and cut short unpleasant ones. This study finds recurrent, scalable patterns in human approach and avoidance behavior. The paper quantifies the push and pull of motivation. The patterns reveal the hidden mathematics of human motivation.
plos-pone-0010713: Fly flight muscles need precise protein ratios. This study shows the protein CF2 represses actin 88F to maintain filament balance in developing flight muscle. The paper reveals a regulator of muscle architecture. The filament balance keeps the wings beating strong.
plos-pone-0010813: People born with TP53 mutations face steep cancer odds. This cohort study tests whether MDM2, MDM4, and codon-72 variants shift cancer risk in these carriers. The paper refines personal risk estimates. The findings could tailor surveillance for high-risk families. The modifiers matter for genetic counseling.
plos-pone-0010913: A cloudy lens steals sight — and a short surgery restores it. This longitudinal study tracks how cataract surgery changes daily activities and time use in Kenya, Bangladesh, and the Philippines. The paper quantifies restored lives. The data champion global eye care.
plos-pone-0011013: Pet dogs with bone cancer can guide human therapy. This comparative oncology study tracks rapamycin's pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics in dogs with osteosarcoma. The paper bridges species. The data inform human trial dosing. The cross-species bridge speeds drugs to patients.
plos-pone-0011113: Yeast cells ship tiny vesicles into their surroundings. This study characterizes yeast extracellular vesicles and the multiple cellular-traffic pathways that build them. The paper reveals vesicle biogenesis. The finding informs cell biology and biotechnology. The pathways mirror those in human cells.
plos-pone-0011213: In Côte d'Ivoire, HIV treatment is free but sickness still bankrupts. This study quantifies the financial burden of morbidity for HIV-infected adults on antiretroviral therapy. The paper exposes out-of-pocket costs. The finding argues for broader health coverage. The coverage would protect fragile households.
plos-pone-0011313: A tweaked tomato gene fends off two viruses. This study shows an induced mutation in tomato eIF4E leads to immunity to two potyviruses. The paper offers a crop-protection strategy. The finding informs plant breeding. The informed breeding grows hardier tomatoes.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1213:
Patrick Hurley, the American ambassador in China, wrote to the Secretary of State and to Ambassador Harriman in Moscow on 19 July 1945. Hurley dealt with the China file: a Nationalist government at war, a communist rival in the north, and American hopes for a joined front.

Sending one dispatch to both the secretary and the Moscow envoy tied the China and Soviet files together. Soviet moves in Asia bore hard on China's future, as all three men knew. This cable shows that link being worked in practice. It is Washington's China hand writing to its Russia hand, mid-summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1313:
Secretary of War Stimson wrote to the President on 30 July 1945. The letter came in the summit's final days. By then Truman had been fully briefed on the atomic test, and the terms to Japan had gone out with the weapon held behind them.

A war secretary's letter at that hour carried the counsel of the man who had overseen the bomb from its birth. Stimson's advice joined the military and moral weight of the choices ahead. This message is part of the last counsel the president received at Potsdam. It shows the cabinet's elder hand still on the brief at the close.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1413:
Secretary Byrnes answered Ambassador Caffery in Paris on 15 August 1945. The reply came nine days after Caffery's great cluster of cables to the secretary. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Replies from the secretary close the loop that cables open. After reading Caffery's six messages of 6 August, readers reach Byrnes's answer with a sense of what Washington decided to give, refuse, or postpone. The date matters too: 15 August was the day the war against Japan ended. So the reply belongs to the first day of the postwar world. The French file, like everything else, turned a page that day.
frus-1945-50-intel-d13:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff sent a joint memorandum to Secretary of War Henry Stimson and Secretary of the Navy Forrestal on 19 September 1945. It carried the settled view of the nation's top military body. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

When the Joint Chiefs spoke together, the armed services presented one front to the civilians above them. Their memorandum on the eve of the OSS order shows the military claiming its share in whatever intelligence system came next. Readers should weigh the channel: the chiefs wrote to both service secretaries at once, binding Army and Navy to a common line. Much of the volume's later bargaining grows from positions fixed in papers like this.
frus-1945-50-intel-d113:
Hoyt Vandenberg, the new director of central intelligence, wrote to Hoover on 3 July 1946. Vandenberg had taken over the CIG in June, full of plans to make it a real agency. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Vandenberg's arrival changed the group's pace: he wanted the SSU's operations, a bigger budget, and a clear field abroad. His first letters to Hoover opened the sharpest phase of the border war with the FBI. Readers should watch the difference in tone from Souers's careful papers. Where Souers conciliated, Vandenberg pressed. The volume's second half runs on the friction his pressing created, with departments, with the bureau, and with the White House itself.
frus-1945-50-intel-d213:
A memorandum dated 9 May 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Chief of the Legislative Liaison Division, Central Intelligence Group (Pforzheimer). The reader was the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter). It is document 213 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d313:
A letter from Secretary of Defense Johnson reached Secretary of State Acheson on 7 October 1949. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 313 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. Two years into the CIA's life, the question in these papers is less how to build it than how to fix it.

Between offices that did not answer to each other, a letter was the polite but firm way to press a point. Many of the big fights of these years can be followed letter by letter. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d413:
John Steelman, acting chairman of the National Security Resources Board, wrote to Sidney Souers of the National Security Council on 2 February 1950. The memo is document 413 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The Resources Board planned how the nation's farms, plants, and workers would serve in a war. Its place in an intelligence volume shows how wide the word security had grown by 1950. Steelman's memo links war planning at home with the secret work of watching threats abroad. The Board's link to the Council gave its chairman a direct line into war planning at the top.
frus-1861-d13:
Norman Judd, the American minister to Prussia, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 July 1861. The dispatch is document 13 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Judd was a friend of Lincoln's from Illinois politics, sent to Berlin that spring. Prussia was rising as the strong power of north Germany, and its stance mattered. Judd's reports told Washington how the Berlin court read the American war in its first summer. Berlin watched the war through the lens of its own struggle with Austria and France. Berlin's cool tone suited the Union, which asked no more than strict fairness.
frus-1861-d113:
Mr. Jones wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 July 1861. The dispatch is document 113 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Jones wrote on the eve of Bull Run, the war's first great battle. His July report is the second of his two papers in this file. Read with his April note, it brackets the season in which the short war became a long one. His two reports, spring and summer, frame the war's first season from one post. One post, two seasons: the frame shows how much the war had changed by July.
frus-1861-d213:
The State Department sent word to Mr. Marsh on 21 June 1861, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 213 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It was written in the opening months of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d13:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 4 February 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 13 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the winter of the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d113:
Writing home was Charles Francis Adams's duty, and his letter of 31 July 1862 went to Seward. Congress received it as Document 113 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d213:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons on 5 April 1862, in a note printed as Document 213 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Lyons, the British minister in Washington, received it at the legation.

Early April 1862 brought the great battle of Shiloh in Tennessee and the start of the campaign against Richmond. Each swing of the war changed the odds that Europe might step in, so envoys traded paper at a fast rate. A note from this week sits in the file as part of that quick, watchful exchange. Each note was numbered and docketed by clerks, which is why the file reads so evenly.
frus-1862-d313:
On 20 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William L. Dayton another dispatch, printed as Document 313 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Three letters in two days mark the post-battle rush.

Seward wrote on the eve of Lincoln's emancipation announcement, which he had helped shape and knew was coming. The proclamation would give the war a cause that European publics could cheer. His letters to Paris in these days prepared his envoy for the new ground, on which defending the Union also meant defending freedom. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d413:
From Madrid on 9 November 1861, Carl Schurz sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 413 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed to accompany the President's annual message.

Schurz wrote in the weeks when Britain, France, and Spain had just agreed to act together in Mexico, a move that worried Washington deeply. As minister in Madrid he could watch Spanish motives at close range. His reports home fed the Union's effort to keep the European powers separate and neutral. The dispatch is part of the first season of that long campaign, before Schurz left Spain for army service.
frus-1862-d513:
Two days after Pike's latest report was dated, on 8 August 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to James Shepherd Pike. It is Document 513 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The crossed dates are the Atlantic mail at work: each man wrote from news the other had not seen. Seward's August orders to The Hague kept up the standing themes of Dutch neutrality and colonial ports. They also kept up the Union's refusal to treat the rebellion as a nation. Pike's replies, arriving a month later, show how those themes landed. The pair of files, order and report interleaved, is the true shape of the record the volume preserves. It is a slow conversation. Two governments carried it on in good faith across an ocean.
frus-1862-d613:
The Danish file opens on 22 January 1862 with this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Bradford R. Wood, the American minister at Copenhagen. It is Document 613 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Denmark was a small maritime kingdom. Its ports and its Sound dues touched Baltic trade. Wood, a New York lawyer, held the post through the war. Seward's opening order set out the Union's case for the Copenhagen court. The Baltic was far from the fighting, but its states' goodwill counted in the general European balance the Department tracked. The letter begins a quiet, regular file in the volume's northern tier.
frus-1862-d713:
Luis Molina wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 September 1862. Molina was Costa Rica's envoy in Washington, a lawyer who had long handled his land's affairs in the United States. The letter is document 713 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Foreign envoys in Washington wrote to Seward on the business between their lands and the United States. For Costa Rica, trade and the transit routes of Central America were never far from the talks. Molina's letter is part of that formal exchange, in which small republics dealt with a great power then fighting for its life. The file that follows shows the talk run both ways.
frus-1863p1-d13:
On 13 December 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The letter is document 13 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. Seward wrote on the day of the battle of Fredericksburg, though its news had not yet reached London.

Letters crossed the Atlantic in about ten days by steamer, so each side wrote in the dark about the other's last moves. Seward's mail set the claims Adams was to press on Britain. They were fair dealing, a tight rein on warships built for the South, and no aid to the rebellion. This letter is one link in that chain of orders.
frus-1863p1-d113:
On 11 March 1863, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the first of three letters to him dated that day in the volume. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 113 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Three letters in a day, a week after a batch of twelve, show a desk that never let the London file cool. Seward split his points across the sheets so Adams could use each on its own. This one opens the day's set. It is part of the spring press on Britain, kept up sheet by sheet from Washington.
frus-1863p1-d213:
The mail from London dated 11 June 1863 brought Secretary of State William H. Seward this report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as document 213 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Confederate agents were busy in Britain buying ships, arms, and supplies. Reports from the London legation fed Washington's protests against that trade. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d313:
To Mr. Stuart of the British legation in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote on 3 November 1862. The note is document 313 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Stuart served at the British legation in Washington and handled business with the State Department when the minister himself was away or occupied. His notes form part of the same Anglo-American exchange. It comes from the autumn after Antietam, when Lincoln's first emancipation order had just raised the stakes for Britain. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d413: Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 March 1863. It is document 413 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, among the formal British papers in the Civil War correspondence. Through such notes London lodged protests and guarded its neutral rights against Union measures at sea.
frus-1863p1-d513:
A dispatch dated 14 May 1863 went from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to William H. Seward, Secretary of State. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d613:
Document 613, dated 14 August 1863, records a letter from Assistant Secretary of State F. W. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the late summer of 1863.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
plos-pone-0000113:
Avihay Apatoff, Eddo Kim, and Yossef Kliger published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. It tackles a practical problem in bioinformatics. The question is how to judge whether computer tools that detect homology, shared ancestry between proteins, do a good job.

Most checks of these tools lean on sequence alignment, which can bias the score. The authors work toward a scoring approach that does not depend on alignment, so different detection methods can be compared on fair terms. A cleaner yardstick helps researchers pick tools they can trust when hunting for distant protein relatives.
plos-pone-0000213:
Joana M. Ramis, Clara Collart, and James C. Smith published this developmental biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. In the frog Xenopus, signals called Xnrs and activin guide early development. The authors show the two signals regulate distinct sets of genes, and that activin in particular controls cell division during development.

An embryo must grow and pattern itself at the same time, and these signals help divide that labor. Separating which genes each signal controls clarifies how a ball of cells becomes an organized body. The frog work informs developmental biology broadly, since the same signal families pattern human embryos.
plos-pone-0000313:
Benoit Foligne, Georgia Zoumpopoulou, Joelle Dewulf, and colleagues published this probiotics study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Probiotics are live microbes eaten for health benefits, and how they work has been unclear. The authors report a key role for dendritic cells, the immune system's scouts, in how probiotics produce their effects.

Dendritic cells sample the gut and teach the rest of the immune system what to tolerate. If probiotics act through them, that explains benefits that reach beyond the gut itself. The paper gives the probiotic field a concrete mechanism to test, in place of vague claims about good bacteria.
plos-pone-0000413:
Sara Calhim, Simone Immler, and Tim R. Birkhead connected sperm shape to mating competition in birds, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. After mating, sperm from rival males can compete inside the female, a pressure called postcopulatory sexual selection. The team asked whether species facing stronger competition have more uniform sperm.

Their title states the pattern they found: strong postcopulatory selection goes with reduced variation in sperm morphology. Uniform sperm suggests selection is fine-tuning the design tightly where competition is fierce. Bird sperm vary hugely across species, so this link helps explain what drives that variety, a long-standing puzzle in evolutionary biology.
plos-pone-0000513:
Marcelo M.S. Lima and colleagues examined a small brain region's command over sleep in rats, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The region is the substantia nigra pars compacta, better known for its role in movement and its loss in Parkinson's disease. The team studied its role in regulating sleep patterns.

Parkinson's patients famously suffer disturbed sleep, and the link is usually blamed on other brain systems. If this movement center also regulates sleep, the two symptom families share one source. Rat studies let researchers manipulate the region directly and watch sleep architecture change, something impossible to do as cleanly in patients.
plos-pone-0000613:
Themba Mzilahowa, Philip J. McCall and Ian M. Hastings examined the genetics of Plasmodium falciparum, the parasite that causes the most dangerous form of malaria. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study tackles a live dispute about how the parasite's populations are structured. The title gives their answer plainly: the organism is essentially sexual in its reproduction.

How fast malaria can adapt matters for every drug and vaccine aimed at it. If parasite genes mix freely through sexual reproduction, new traits can spread in ways that control programs must plan for. The authors set out their evidence for that mixing. Malaria workers and population geneticists alike will find the argument worth weighing.
plos-pone-0000713:
Patrick Hossler, Bhanu Chandra Mulukutla and Wei-Shou Hu analyzed how mammalian cells process sugar chains on proteins, in PLOS ONE in 2007. N-glycosylation, the attachment of those chains, is key to the quality of many therapeutic glycoprotein drugs. A relatively small set of enzymes gives rise to a large number of N-glycans through a network of reactions and intermediates.

A systems analysis treats that network whole, rather than enzyme by enzyme. For drug makers, the exact sugar pattern on a protein can decide whether a medicine works and how long it lasts. Modeling the network points to which steps to tune in the cells that manufacture biologics.
plos-pone-0000813:
Kenji Matsuura, Takashi Tamura, Norimasa Kobayashi and colleagues unmasked the chemical signal termites use to recognize their eggs, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Social insects rely heavily on pheromone communication to maintain their social life. Egg protection is among the most fundamental social behaviors in social insects. A fungus that mimics termite eggs, nicknamed the termite-ball, had recently been discovered, opening the study of egg recognition.

Their title names the pheromone: lysozyme, a protein better known for killing bacteria. Workers apparently read lysozyme on eggs as a do-not-eat, protect-this signal. A defensive enzyme doubling as a social label is an elegant economy, and a caution for pest control by mimicry.
plos-pone-0000913:
Diana Abdueva, Michele Wing, Betty Schaub and colleagues put two Affymetrix gene chips head to head, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Gene chips let labs read the activity of thousands of genes at once. The newer exon arrays promised whole genome readings at the level of single exons, the segments that get stitched into messages.

That design dropped some older features and used a new way to prepare samples. The team ran an experimental comparison against the widely used U133Plus2 array. Head to head tests like this help labs decide whether a new platform earns its claims. They also protect later studies from building on a weaker tool.
plos-pone-0001013:
Tim Schulz, Markus Glaubitz, Doreen Kuhlow and colleagues warned that a common mouse engineering tool can switch off without warning, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The Cre and loxP system lets researchers delete a gene in one tissue only, a standard route to knockout mice. Studies often check a tail sample to confirm the system is present.

The team report losing Cre expression in a transgenic line, which makes tail checks unreliable. A mouse can carry the gene yet not express it where it counts. Their report is a practical warning: verify the tool itself, not just its paperwork. Many published results rest on this system.
plos-pone-0001113:

Genomic studies had usually analyzed each protein as one unit, averaging change across its whole length.

The authors argue the targets of adaptation may sit in particular parts: domains, or regions tied to folding. In Drosophila simulans they report rampant adaptive evolution in regions of unknown function. Unknown does not mean unimportant; it may mean the most interesting biology is unmapped. plos-pone-0001213:

The authors report that HCF-1 proteins regulate the status of this mark, which is tied to chromosome behavior during division. HCF-1 was first found through herpes simplex virus, where it helps switch the virus on. Its epigenetic role in normal cells is the subject here.
plos-pone-0001313:

Joseph Bauer and colleagues tested it alongside standard chemotherapy agents, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The compound induces apoptosis through one pathway and inhibits survival signaling in cancer cells.

The authors report that nitrosylcobalamin potentiates the anti-neoplastic effects of chemotherapeutic agents via suppression of survival signaling. plos-pone-0001413:
Maria Allhorn and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how a strep germ blunts human antibodies. The germ makes an enzyme that cuts the sugar chain on human IgG, a key class of antibody. Cut antibodies bind less well to receptors on white blood cells. That weakens the push to eat and kill germs.

The authors show how this sugar cut changes the bond between antibodies and their receptors. The change is enough to damp the immune attack. Learning this trick helps explain how strep germs slip past defense. It may also guide drugs that block the enzyme and restore antibody power.
plos-pone-0001513:

They chart gains, losses, and splits of the gene's parts over time. The locus grew more complex without simple copying. Such cases broaden the tale of how scent sense evolves. Scent genes shape mating and food choice, so their change can split species apart.
plos-pone-0001613:

They show the fly protein steers the splicing of a muscle protein and also shapes cell death. Those twin roles mirror the human protein's reach. A fly model with shared roles lets labs screen drugs fast. Hits there can then be sifted for the human disease.
plos-pone-0001713:

plos-pone-0001813:

plos-pone-0001913:

The team ran computer simulations with known histories, then scored how well each method rebuilt them. A fair race on fake data with known truth shows which tools to trust on real data. plos-pone-0002013:

plos-pone-0002113:

plos-pone-0002213:

plos-pone-0002313:
